Appendix H Identification of the worker’s parameters and regime tests

H.1 Theoretically principled method

To use Theorem 3.2 for empirical analysis, we need to recover (α^,β^)(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}) from data on the worker’s behavior. The two parameters are separately identified if the same worker population is observed paired with two AI systems that differ in their overlap with the human’s evidence. We refer to a (worker population, AI system, task) configuration with parameters (τH,τA,λ)(\tau_{H},\tau_{A},\lambda) as a deployment, and assume the analyst observes data from two deployments dd and d′d^{\prime} (e.g., the same workers paired with GPT-4o on dd and Llama on d′d^{\prime}, on the same task) that share the worker population but differ in overlap: λd≠λd′\lambda^{d}\neq\lambda^{d^{\prime}}. The distinguishing property of BR vs. CN (§2.2) provides the identification lever: at BR, the worker’s AI weight wAw_{A} depends on λ\lambda (she corrects for overlap); at CN, wAw_{A} does not (she treats the AI signal as independent). Across two deployments with λd≠λd′\lambda^{d}\neq\lambda^{d^{\prime}}, the difference in wAw_{A} is informative about α^\hat{\alpha}.

Definition H.1 (Cross-deployment AI-weight ratio).

RA​(α^,β^,d,d′):=wAd​(α^,β^)/wAd′​(α^,β^)R_{A}\left(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta};d,d^{\prime}\right):=w_{A}^{d}\left(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}\right)/w_{A}^{d^{\prime}}\left(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}\right), with wAd,wAd′w_{A}^{d},w_{A}^{d^{\prime}} from Lemma 2.4. The empirical analogue is R^A:=w^Ad/w^Ad′\hat{R}_{A}:=\hat{w}_{A}^{d}/\hat{w}_{A}^{d^{\prime}}, where w^Ad,w^Ad′\hat{w}_{A}^{d},\hat{w}_{A}^{d^{\prime}} are estimated within each deployment d:=(τH,τAd,λd),d′:=(τH,τAd′,λd′)d:=(\tau_{H},\tau_{A}^{d},\lambda^{d}),d^{\prime}:=(\tau_{H},\tau_{A}^{d^{\prime}},\lambda^{d^{\prime}}).

Proposition H.2 (Cross-deployment signature).

Under Assumption 2.3,

  • •

    Correlation neglect (α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0, any β^>0\hat{\beta}>0): RACN=1R_{A}^{\mathrm{CN}}=1.

  • •

    Best response (α^=1,β^=1\hat{\alpha}=1,\hat{\beta}=1): When λd≠λd′\lambda^{d}\neq\lambda^{d^{\prime}}, RABR≠1R_{A}^{\mathrm{BR}}\neq 1 generically.

  • •

    Interior (α^∈(0,1)\hat{\alpha}\in\left(0,1\right)): RAR_{A} is continuous in α^\hat{\alpha}, and RA≠1R_{A}\neq 1 generically. Moreover, when λd≠λd′\lambda^{d}\neq\lambda^{d^{\prime}}, RA​(α^)R_{A}\left(\hat{\alpha}\right) is locally invertible near α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0 with partial derivative λd′−λd≠0\lambda^{d^{\prime}}-\lambda^{d}\neq 0.

The empirical R^A\hat{R}_{A} thus separates correlation-neglect workers from best-response workers, and locally identifies an interior α^\hat{\alpha} near correlation neglect.

Two-step identification.

Step 1 (recover α^\hat{\alpha} from R^A\hat{R}_{A}). Compute the BR-predicted ratio from deployment parameters (τH,τAd,λd)(\tau_{H},\tau_{A}^{d},\lambda^{d}), (τH,τAd′,λd′)(\tau_{H},\tau_{A}^{d^{\prime}},\lambda^{d^{\prime}}),

RABR​(d,d′)=(1−λd)/(τH−τAd(λd)2)(1−λd′)/(τH−τAd′(λd′)2),\displaystyle\textstyle R_{A}^{\mathrm{BR}}\left(d,d^{\prime}\right)=\frac{\left.\left(1-\lambda^{d}\right)\middle/\left(\tau_{H}-\tau_{A}^{d}\left(\lambda^{d}\right)^{2}\right)\right.}{\left.\left(1-\lambda^{d^{\prime}}\right)\middle/\left(\tau_{H}-\tau_{A}^{d^{\prime}}\left(\lambda^{d^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\right)\right.},

and compare to R^A\hat{R}_{A}: R^A≈1\hat{R}_{A}\approx 1 supports α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0, R^A≈RABR\hat{R}_{A}\approx R_{A}^{\mathrm{BR}} supports α^=1\hat{\alpha}=1, and intermediate values can pin down α^∈(0,1)\hat{\alpha}\in\left(0,1\right) by solving

R^A=(1−α^λd)/(τH−τAdα^2(λd)2)(1−α^λd′)/(τH−τAd′α^2(λd′)2).\displaystyle\textstyle\hat{R}_{A}=\frac{\left.\left(1-\hat{\alpha}\lambda^{d}\right)\middle/\left(\tau_{H}-\tau_{A}^{d}\hat{\alpha}^{2}\left(\lambda^{d}\right)^{2}\right)\right.}{\left.\left(1-\hat{\alpha}\lambda^{d^{\prime}}\right)\middle/\left(\tau_{H}-\tau_{A}^{d^{\prime}}\hat{\alpha}^{2}\left(\lambda^{d^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\right)\right.}.

Step 2 (recover β^\hat{\beta} from w^A\hat{w}_{A} given α^\hat{\alpha}). Inverting Lemma 2.4,

β^=w^Ad​τH−τAd​α^2​(λd)2τH​(1−α^​λd).\displaystyle\hat{\beta}=\hat{w}_{A}^{d}\frac{\tau_{H}-\tau_{A}^{d}\hat{\alpha}^{2}\left(\lambda^{d}\right)^{2}}{\tau_{H}\left(1-\hat{\alpha}\lambda^{d}\right)}.

At α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0, this reduces to β^=w^Ad\hat{\beta}=\hat{w}_{A}^{d}: the empirical AI weight estimates trust directly.

Proof of Proposition H.2.

By Lemma 2.4, the worker’s AI weight at deployment dd is

H.2 Implementation details

§H.1 presents the two-step identification result theoretically. In the empirical work of §4 we implement two complementary procedures, both inversions of Lemma 2.4, differing in how the human-side signal ℓH\ell_{H} and the overlap λ\lambda are constructed.

Approach 1: joint inversion using confidence-based ℓH\ell_{H}.

For each deployment d∈{GPT-4o,Llama-3.1-8b}d\in\{\text{GPT-4o},\text{Llama-3.1-8b}\}, fit a logistic regression of FF on (ℓH,ℓA)(\ell_{H},\ell_{A}) with intercept (no regularization, BFGS) on the Has-Rec rows for that deployment, recovering empirical weights (w^Hd,w^Ad)(\hat{w}_{H}^{d},\hat{w}_{A}^{d}). Estimate the conditional-mean primitives by their plug-in moments,

τ^H=12​(ℓH|h​_​a​c​c=1¯−ℓH|h​_​a​c​c=0¯),τ^Ad=12​(ℓA|a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​t=1,d¯−ℓA|a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​t=0,d¯),\textstyle\hat{\tau}_{H}=\tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\overline{\ell_{H}\mid h\_acc=1}-\overline{\ell_{H}\mid h\_acc=0}\right),\qquad\hat{\tau}_{A}^{d}=\tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\overline{\ell_{A}\mid ai\_correct=1,d}-\overline{\ell_{A}\mid ai\_correct=0,d}\right),

treating τ^H\hat{\tau}_{H} as deployment-invariant (the empirical per-deployment values 0.3740.374 and 0.4110.411 agree to within 0.040.04). Then solve the four-equation system from Lemma 2.4,

w^Hd=τ^H−τ^Ad​α^​λ^dτ^H−τ^Ad​α^2​(λ^d)2,w^Ad=β^⋅τ^H​(1−α^​λ^d)τ^H−τ^Ad​α^2​(λ^d)2,d∈{GPT,Llama},\textstyle\hat{w}_{H}^{d}=\frac{\hat{\tau}_{H}-\hat{\tau}_{A}^{d}\,\hat{\alpha}\,\hat{\lambda}^{d}}{\hat{\tau}_{H}-\hat{\tau}_{A}^{d}\,\hat{\alpha}^{2}(\hat{\lambda}^{d})^{2}},\qquad\hat{w}_{A}^{d}=\hat{\beta}\cdot\frac{\hat{\tau}_{H}(1-\hat{\alpha}\,\hat{\lambda}^{d})}{\hat{\tau}_{H}-\hat{\tau}_{A}^{d}\,\hat{\alpha}^{2}(\hat{\lambda}^{d})^{2}},\qquad d\in\{\text{GPT},\text{Llama}\},

for the four unknowns (α^,β^,λ^GPT,λ^Llama)(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta},\hat{\lambda}^{\text{GPT}},\hat{\lambda}^{\text{Llama}}) by trust-region-reflective nonlinear least squares with bounds α^∈[0,1]\hat{\alpha}\in[0,1], β^∈(0,5]\hat{\beta}\in(0,5], λ^d∈[0,0.99]\hat{\lambda}^{d}\in[0,0.99], and 100100 random restarts. The global minimizer is

α^=0.315,β^=0.285,λ^GPT=0.478,λ^Llama=0.365,SSR=5.5×10−3.\textstyle\hat{\alpha}=0.315,\quad\hat{\beta}=0.285,\quad\hat{\lambda}^{\text{GPT}}=0.478,\quad\hat{\lambda}^{\text{Llama}}=0.365,\quad\mathrm{SSR}=5.5\times 10^{-3}.

A 200200-replication non-parametric bootstrap gives β^∈[0.246,0.322]\hat{\beta}\in[0.246,0.322] at the 95%95\% level.

Approach 2: λ^\hat{\lambda} from cross-question variation.

This procedure replaces ℓH\ell_{H} with the per-question signal ℓHHq\ell_{H}^{H_{q}} from §G and estimates λ\lambda directly as the within-YY pooled covariance,

λ^d:=∑y∈{0,1}nd,yCov^(ℓHHq,ℓA∣Y=y,d)∑y∈{0,1}nd,y​Var^​(ℓA∣Y=y,d),\textstyle\hat{\lambda}^{d}:=\frac{\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}n_{d,y}\,\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\ell_{H}^{H_{q}},\ell_{A}\mid Y=y,d)}{\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}n_{d,y}\,\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\ell_{A}\mid Y=y,d)},

mirroring the population identity λ=Cov⁡(ℓH,ℓA∣Y)/Var⁡(ℓA∣Y)\lambda=\mathrm{Cov}(\ell_{H},\ell_{A}\mid Y)/\mathrm{Var}(\ell_{A}\mid Y) implied by Lemma 2.1. We obtain

λ^GPT=0.071∈[0.041,0.100]95%,λ^Llama=0.127∈[0.100,0.154]95%,\textstyle\hat{\lambda}^{\text{GPT}}=0.071\in[0.041,0.100]_{95\%},\qquad\hat{\lambda}^{\text{Llama}}=0.127\in[0.100,0.154]_{95\%},

with both bootstrap CIs strictly above zero. We then re-run the per-deployment logistic regressions of FF on (ℓHHq,ℓA)(\ell_{H}^{H_{q}},\ell_{A}) to obtain weights under this finer signal, and solve the analogous system for (α^,β^)(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}) with λ^d\hat{\lambda}^{d} now treated as plug-in. The resulting fit gives β^=0.254\hat{\beta}=0.254, in close agreement with Approach 1.

On the discrepancy in α^\hat{\alpha}.

The two approaches agree on β^\hat{\beta} (the headline parameter) but not on α^\hat{\alpha}: Approach 1 gives an interior α^=0.315\hat{\alpha}=0.315, Approach 2 returns α^=1\hat{\alpha}=1 at the upper bound. We interpret this as evidence that α^\hat{\alpha} is weakly identified by these moments — small differences in how ℓH\ell_{H} is constructed propagate through the nonlinear inversion to large differences in the α^\hat{\alpha} point estimate. The qualitative claim that α^>0\hat{\alpha}>0 (strict correlation neglect rejected) is robust across approaches and across three direct tests:

  1. (i)

    Approach 1’s residual sum of squares jumps 141141-fold when α^=0\hat{\alpha}=0 is forced.

  2. (ii)

    A likelihood-ratio test of whether |ℓA||\ell_{A}| adds information beyond 4-cell (h​_​a​c​c,a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​t)(h\_acc,ai\_correct) fixed effects gives χ2​(1)=3.93\chi^{2}(1)=3.93, p=0.048p=0.048.

  3. (iii)

    Approach 2’s direct λ^d\hat{\lambda}^{d} are strictly positive in 100%100\% of bootstrap samples for both deployments.

On the discrepancy in λ^\hat{\lambda}.

Both approaches yield positive estimates of overlap, but differ in their relative ordering across the two AIs. We adopt Approach 2 as our primary measure, as it estimates overlap directly from the conditional covariance structure of human and AI signals, rather than indirectly through a nonlinear inversion of worker behavior.

Robustness of β^\hat{\beta}.

Varying the clipping constant ϵ∈{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.02}\epsilon\in\{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.02\} (§G) shifts β^\hat{\beta} across [0.22,0.37][0.22,0.37] but leaves it well below 11 at every value, so the rejection of β^=1\hat{\beta}=1 is robust. A worker-cluster bootstrap that resamples the 315315 workers (rather than 2,1992{,}199 rows i.i.d.) gives β^∈[0.241,0.332]\hat{\beta}\in[0.241,0.332] at the 95%95\% level, slightly wider than the row-bootstrap CI but with the same qualitative conclusion across all three headline quantities (GAP\mathrm{GAP}, β^\hat{\beta}, λ^Llama−λ^GPT\hat{\lambda}^{\text{Llama}}-\hat{\lambda}^{\text{GPT}}).

Test for 𝒜H​A\mathcal{A}_{HA} versus 𝒜A​I\mathcal{A}_{AI}.

Regime classification in Table 1 compares team accuracy 𝒜H​A\mathcal{A}_{HA} to AI accuracy 𝒜A​I\mathcal{A}_{AI} on the same observations. Define the discordant pair counts

n10d:=|{i∈d:Fi=1,ai_correcti=0}|,n01d:=|{i∈d:Fi=0,ai_correcti=1}|.\textstyle n_{10}^{d}:=|\{i\in d:F_{i}=1,\,ai\_correct_{i}=0\}|,\qquad n_{01}^{d}:=|\{i\in d:F_{i}=0,\,ai\_correct_{i}=1\}|.

Under H0:𝒜H​A=𝒜A​IH_{0}:\mathcal{A}_{HA}=\mathcal{A}_{AI}, the conditional distribution of n10dn_{10}^{d} given n10d+n01dn_{10}^{d}+n_{01}^{d} is Binomial⁡(n10d+n01d,12)\mathrm{Binomial}(n_{10}^{d}+n_{01}^{d},\tfrac{1}{2}). The reported pp-values are exact two-sided binomial pp-values from this conditional distribution (the exact form of the McNemar test). The relevant counts are (n10GPT,n01GPT)=(51,89)(n_{10}^{\text{GPT}},n_{01}^{\text{GPT}})=(51,89) and (n10Llama,n01Llama)=(74,66)(n_{10}^{\text{Llama}},n_{01}^{\text{Llama}})=(74,66). We classify a deployment as automation if the test rejects in favor of n01>n10n_{01}>n_{10}, complementarity if it rejects in favor of n10>n01n_{10}>n_{01}, and boundary otherwise.

Appendix I Capability-versus-behavior decomposition

The cross-deployment GAP gap of +0.081+0.081 admits two non-exclusive interpretations: (i) AI-capability composition — different fractions of pairs in each (h​_​a​c​c,a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​t)(h\_acc,ai\_correct) cell across deployments — or (ii) workers responding differently to the two AIs at the per-cell level. We separate them by holding worker behavior at the pooled per-cell rate Pr^​(F=1∣h​_​a​c​c,a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​t)\widehat{\Pr}(F=1\mid h\_acc,ai\_correct) across both deployments and letting only the cell composition vary by AI.

Counterfactual GAP gap.

Let p¯(h,a):=Pr^​(F=1∣h​_​a​c​c=h,a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​t=a)\bar{p}_{(h,a)}:=\widehat{\Pr}(F=1\mid h\_acc=h,ai\_correct=a) on the pooled Has-Rec sample. For each deployment dd, define the counterfactual team accuracy

𝒜H​Ad,cf:=∑h,a∈{0,1}Pr^d​(h​_​a​c​c=h,a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​t=a)⋅p¯(h,a),\textstyle\mathcal{A}_{HA}^{d,\mathrm{cf}}:=\sum_{h,a\in\{0,1\}}\widehat{\Pr}_{d}(h\_acc=h,\,ai\_correct=a)\cdot\bar{p}_{(h,a)},

which assigns the pooled per-cell behavior to deployment dd’s observed cell composition. The capability share is the ratio of the counterfactual GAP gap (driven by composition alone) to the observed GAP gap:

CapShare:=(𝒜H​AGPT,cf−𝒜HGPT)−(𝒜H​ALlama,cf−𝒜HLlama)GAPGPT−GAPLlama.\textstyle\mathrm{CapShare}:=\frac{(\mathcal{A}_{HA}^{\text{GPT},\mathrm{cf}}-\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\text{GPT}})-(\mathcal{A}_{HA}^{\text{Llama},\mathrm{cf}}-\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\text{Llama}})}{\mathrm{GAP}^{\text{GPT}}-\mathrm{GAP}^{\text{Llama}}}.

The point estimate is CapShare=92.6%\mathrm{CapShare}=92.6\%. A non-parametric row bootstrap with 1,0001{,}000 replications gives a median of 93.2%93.2\% and a 95% confidence interval of [68%,148%][68\%,148\%]. The wide upper end reflects the fact that the denominator GAPGPT−GAPLlama\mathrm{GAP}^{\text{GPT}}-\mathrm{GAP}^{\text{Llama}} is itself a small estimated quantity (+0.081+0.081); the lower bound stays well above 50%50\% across resamples.

Direct test of behavioral homogeneity.

A complementary test compares two logistic regressions of FF on (h​_​a​c​c,a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​t)(h\_acc,ai\_correct) cell fixed effects: a reduced model with no AI interaction versus a full model interacting cell with deployment. The likelihood-ratio statistic is χ2​(4)=0.96\chi^{2}(4)=0.96 (p=0.92p=0.92); we cannot reject the null that workers respond identically to the two AIs at the per-cell level. The capability-share decomposition and the LR test thus point in the same direction: the cross-deployment welfare difference is driven primarily by the composition of (h​_​a​c​c,a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​t)(h\_acc,ai\_correct) pairs each AI generates, not by deployment-specific worker behavior.

Appendix J Overlap heterogeneity across AIs and subjects

The direct λ^d\hat{\lambda}^{d} estimator from Approach 2 of §H can be applied at finer-than-deployment granularity, by restricting the within-YY covariance computation to subsets of the Has-Rec sample. We report two cuts.

Across AIs.

Pooled across all subjects, λ^GPT=0.071\hat{\lambda}^{\text{GPT}}=0.071 and λ^Llama=0.127\hat{\lambda}^{\text{Llama}}=0.127, a difference of +0.056+0.056. A row bootstrap on the difference gives a 95% CI of [+0.015,+0.097][+0.015,+0.097] (two-sided p≈0.009p\approx 0.009), with 99.7%99.7\% of 1,0001{,}000 resamples having λ^Llama>λ^GPT\hat{\lambda}^{\text{Llama}}>\hat{\lambda}^{\text{GPT}}. The smaller AI’s evidence overlaps more with what humans access on the same questions; this is consistent with the cue-pool reading of §2, in which a smaller model relies more heavily on cues that humans also access while a larger model contributes more genuinely novel evidence.

Across subjects.

The Has-Rec sample is split as math (n=1,388n=1{,}388), physics (n=497n=497), and moral reasoning (n=314n=314). Direct λ^\hat{\lambda} varies dramatically across subjects, and the same ordering holds within each AI separately:

Subject nn (Has-Rec) GPT-4o λ^\hat{\lambda} Llama λ^\hat{\lambda} Pooled λ^\hat{\lambda}
Math 1,3881{,}388 +0.19+0.19 +0.25+0.25 +0.20+0.20
Physics 497497 +0.04+0.04 +0.07+0.07 +0.04+0.04
Moral 314314 0.00\phantom{+}0.00 0.00\phantom{+}0.00 0.00\phantom{+}0.00
Pooled 2,1992{,}199 +0.07+0.07 +0.13+0.13 +0.08+0.08

Domains where humans and AI rely on shared procedural cues (math) exhibit substantial overlap; domains where reasoning paths are more idiosyncratic (moral reasoning) exhibit essentially none. This provides empirical content for the cue-pool framing: under the model, λ\lambda is a property of the human-domain pair (Proposition 2.2); the data shows the predicted variation across domains and additionally a cross-AI effect that the uniform-sampling model does not predict.

Limitations of these estimates.

Both findings rely on the per-question ℓHHq\ell_{H}^{H_{q}} proxy, which is a population-level signal rather than an individual worker’s signal. Replacing ℓHHq\ell_{H}^{H_{q}} with the confidence-based ℓH\ell_{H} (Approach 1) does not give a directly comparable λ^\hat{\lambda} because the latter has only three values per worker. We report the cross-AI and cross-subject patterns as evidence that λ\lambda varies meaningfully and in interpretable directions, not as precise structural estimates.

Appendix K Empirical welfare evaluation

We evaluate the welfare consequences of trust calibration by simulating a trust-calibrated decision rule. For each observation ii, recall hi:=h​_​a​c​cih_{i}:=h\_acc_{i} indicate whether the human’s unaided answer is correct, ai:=a​i​_​c​o​r​r​e​c​tia_{i}:=ai\_correct_{i} whether the AI’s actual recommendation is correct, and FiF_{i} whether the worker’s final answer is correct. We simulate a reliance policy that chooses between the human’s and AI’s answers, and its accuracy is evaluated against the ground truth of the question.

Constructing the simulated policy.

The policy uses Xi=(ℓHi,ℓAi)X_{i}=(\ell_{H}^{i},\ell_{A}^{i}), where ℓHi\ell_{H}^{i} is constructed from the worker’s stated confidence and ℓAi\ell_{A}^{i} from the AI’s question-level accuracy, as described in Appendix G. These predictors summarize human confidence and AI performance on the question; they do not encode the content of the AI’s specific response.

Within the disagreement sample, define

pHd​(x):=Pr⁡(hi=1∣Xi=x,i∈𝒟d),pAd​(x):=Pr⁡(ai=1∣Xi=x,i∈𝒟d).p_{H}^{d}(x):=\Pr(h_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=x,\ i\in\mathcal{D}_{d}),\qquad p_{A}^{d}(x):=\Pr(a_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=x,\ i\in\mathcal{D}_{d}).

We estimate these conditional correctness probabilities using logistic regression on (ℓH,ℓA)(\ell_{H},\ell_{A}) with five-fold cross-validation. Each observation receives predictions from models fitted on the other four folds.

For each held-out observation, define the reliance score and decision

si:=p^Ad(Xi)−p^Hd(Xi),πi:=𝟏{si>0}.s_{i}:=\hat{p}_{A}^{d}(X_{i})-\hat{p}_{H}^{d}(X_{i}),\qquad\pi_{i}:=\mathbf{1}\{s_{i}>0\}.

The simulated policy submits the AI’s answer when πi=1\pi_{i}=1 and retains the human’s answer otherwise. We fix the threshold at zero rather than selecting it to maximize accuracy on the evaluation observations. With the true conditional probabilities, this rule is optimal among policies choosing between the two answers using XiX_{i}. The fitted logistic rule provides an empirical approximation to this benchmark.

Capability-dependent benefits of trust calibration.

For GPT-4o, the simulated policy raises accuracy from approximately 0.8510.851 to 0.8770.877, bringing the team close to the AI-alone accuracy of 0.8840.884. It follows the AI on approximately 92%92\% of disagreements, compared with the workers’ observed reliance rate of 70%70\%. The policy’s greater reliance and higher accuracy are consistent with a welfare cost from under-trust on the stronger AI.

For Llama-3.1-8b, the observed workers outperform the fitted policy. Within this comparison, replacing their decisions with the coarse-signal rule offers no improvement. The benefits of greater trust therefore depend on AI capability and cannot be assumed to transfer uniformly across deployments.

Information and the limits of the benchmark.

In reality, the worker observes more than the two predictors available to the fitted rule. In particular, she reads the AI’s actual answer and can assess its reasoning and relevance to the question. The question-level accuracy measure averages across responses and omits these response-specific information. Workers’ superior performance relative to the fitted rule in the Llama deployment is consistent with their using this additional information.

The broader implication is that improving human–AI performance may require attention to information as well as behavior. Better-calibrated trust offers a measurable opportunity in the stronger-AI deployment, but a rule based only on coarse confidence and accuracy measures does not capture the worker’s full decision problem. Richer response-specific information would allow a more informative benchmark and a clearer assessment of the remaining scope for behavioral improvement.

Appendix L Departures from theory and what they mean

The framework of §§2–3 is a binary-classification model with a Gaussian generative process, symmetric prior, and linear-rule decision-maker. The empirical setting departs from each of these in ways the analysis must accommodate.

Binary reduction of a four-way task.

ChatBench is a four-way multiple-choice task; the model is binary. We define the outcome YiY_{i} as the indicator that the worker’s chosen letter matches the unique correct letter on item ii, collapsing the three wrong letters into Yi=0Y_{i}=0. Two consequences follow. (i) The model’s closed-form AI accuracy Φ⁡(τ^Ad/2)\Phi(\sqrt{\hat{\tau}_{A}^{d}/2}) does not match empirical accuracy: at τ^ALlama=1.64\hat{\tau}_{A}^{\text{Llama}}=1.64 the formula gives 0.820.82 versus empirical 𝒜A​ILlama=0.787\mathcal{A}_{AI}^{\text{Llama}}=0.787, and at τ^AGPT=2.02\hat{\tau}_{A}^{\text{GPT}}=2.02 it gives 0.840.84 versus empirical 0.8840.884. We do not use the closed-form accuracy formula anywhere in the empirical section; every accuracy reported in §4 and Tables 1 and 2 is the empirical sample mean. (ii) The empirical base rate Pr^​(h​_​a​c​c=1)=0.612\widehat{\Pr}(h\_acc=1)=0.612 is not 0.50.5, so the symmetric-prior assumption underlying Φ⁡(τ^H/2)=Pr⁡(h​_​a​c​c=1)\Phi(\sqrt{\hat{\tau}_{H}/2})=\Pr(h\_acc=1) does not literally hold. We use prior-free conditional-mean estimators for τ^H\hat{\tau}_{H} and τ^Ad\hat{\tau}_{A}^{d} (Appendix H), which are invariant to the base rate.

ℓA\ell_{A} saturation and cross-deployment scale.

About 62%62\% of Has-Rec rows have pAm,q∈{0,1}p_{A}^{m,q}\in\{0,1\} (Appendix G), saturating ℓA\ell_{A} at ±5.293\pm 5.293. Saturation is more severe for GPT-4o, where pAm,q=1p_{A}^{m,q}=1 on the majority of items, than for Llama-3.1-8b. As a consequence, per-deployment regression coefficients w^Ad\hat{w}_{A}^{d} are not on the same scale across deployments: w^AGPT\hat{w}_{A}^{\text{GPT}} effectively measures the response to a near-binary "AI is right" indicator, while w^ALlama\hat{w}_{A}^{\text{Llama}} uses more variation. Approach 1 (§H) absorbs this scale difference through the structural inversion, which divides through τ^Ad\hat{\tau}_{A}^{d} when recovering β^\hat{\beta}. Approach 2 uses cross-question covariance and is invariant to monotone rescaling of ℓA\ell_{A}. Direct comparison of w^Ad\hat{w}_{A}^{d} across deployments would not be valid; the structural recovery of β^\hat{\beta} is.

Cue-pool generative story.

The cue-pool model of §2 motivates λ\lambda as the fraction of the AI’s cues also accessed by the human. Language-model decisions are not literally generated by sampling discrete cues from a finite pool. We do not commit to the cue-pool generative process. The structural objects we estimate — the joint distribution of (ℓH,ℓA,Y)(\ell_{H},\ell_{A},Y) and its summary statistics (τH,τA,λ)(\tau_{H},\tau_{A},\lambda) — are well-defined regardless of the underlying generative process. The cue-pool story provides intuition for the cross-domain λ\lambda heterogeneity in Appendix J, but it is not required for the identification or welfare results.

Between-subjects design.

ChatBench randomizes each worker to exactly one AI, so the GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-8b samples are disjoint worker pools. Cross-deployment comparisons therefore rely on random assignment rather than within-worker variation. Random assignment makes large population-level imbalances unlikely in expectation but does not rule out them in any specific sample. The behavioral-homogeneity test of Appendix I (χ2​(4)=0.96\chi^{2}(4)=0.96, p=0.92p=0.92) provides a direct check: per-cell response rates are statistically indistinguishable across the two AI populations, supporting the cross-deployment comparability of β^\hat{\beta} and other behavioral parameters.

Appendix M Reproducibility

All empirical claims in Section 4 and Appendices G–K are computed by a single self-contained Python script that takes the three raw ChatBench files as input. It reproduces sample construction, signal calibration, the headline findings with bootstrap CIs (1,0001{,}000 direct, 200200 structural, 500500 welfare), all regime, correlation-neglect, capability-share, and λ\lambda-heterogeneity tests, the β^=1\hat{\beta}=1 counterfactual, and three robustness checks (worker-cluster bootstrap on all four headline quantities, ϵ\epsilon sensitivity, 55-fold cross-validated linear ceiling). All seeds are fixed; reference values appear in the script header; total runtime is approximately 44 minutes on a single CPU core. The script will be provided with the camera-ready version.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and introduction state three contributions: a phase diagram in (τA,λ)(\tau_{A},\lambda) partitioning impairment, complementarity, and automation regions; identifiability of (α^,β^)(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}) from cross-deployment variation in overlap; and a welfare decomposition into correlation-neglect and trust-miscalibration costs — which are delivered respectively in Theorem 3.2, Proposition H.2, and Proposition 3.4, and instantiated empirically on ChatBench in §4.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: Appendix L enumerates the main limitations of the empirical study as departures from the theoretical model.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: All theoretical results are stated with full assumptions. Complete proofs are given in Appendices A and the proof sections referenced from §2 and §3.

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: Appendix G fully describes sample construction; Appendix H specifies the estimation procedures; Appendix M describes reproducibility details.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

Justification: Headline empirical claims in §4 (e.g., GAP=+0.213\mathrm{GAP}=+0.213, β^=0.285\hat{\beta}=0.285, λ^Llama−λ^GPT=+0.056\hat{\lambda}^{\text{Llama}}-\hat{\lambda}^{\text{GPT}}=+0.056) are reported with 95%95\% non-parametric bootstrap confidence intervals; and a worker-cluster bootstrap is reported in Appendix H as a robustness check.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: The framework’s positive design implications are stated in §4 and §3. On the negative side, the analysis quantifies regimes where adding an AI assistant degrades worker accuracy, which cautions against blanket deployment. The paper introduces no new model or dataset with foreseeable misuse pathways.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).
